in.mechanism: The two-year is mostly an average of what the Fed is expected to do, so it follows the policy rate closely and leads it at turns.
in.why: the source sits still between decisions, so its day-to-day changes are almost all zero and a correlation on them means nothing

out.mechanism: The ten-year contains the expected path of short rates, so the front end pulls it — but only partly, since the rest is term premium.
The curve is the ten-year minus the two-year, so the front end rising flattens it by construction.

node.label: US 2-year yield
node.up: The market expects the Fed to keep rates higher for longer
node.what: What the government pays to borrow for two years. It is mostly a bet on what the Fed will do over that window, so it moves on policy expectations rather than on anything structural.

path.mechanism: Technology profits sit further in the future than the market's, so discounting them harder costs more. This is the same edge as the S&P one, with a longer lever.

path.breaks: Fails when the yield is rising because the US is the problem — a fiscal scare pushes yields up and the dollar down at the same time, which is the tell that it is a credibility story rather than a rate story.
path.mechanism: Money chases yield across borders. A higher US yield relative to everywhere else pulls capital into dollars to earn it.

path.breaks: Reverses when yields are rising because growth is strong — early in a recovery both go up together, and reading that as a warning is the classic mistake.
path.mechanism: A higher discount rate makes every future dollar of profit worth less today. Nothing about the businesses changed; the arithmetic under them did.

path.breaks: Regime-dependent and frequently absent. Bitcoin has rallied through rising-yield stretches more than once, and when it does the liquidity and adoption stories are simply larger than the discount-rate one.
path.mechanism: Bitcoin has no cash flow to discount, so it competes head-on with the risk-free rate: the more a government bond pays for doing nothing, the higher the bar for holding something that pays nothing at all.
